title: Seat a click-type torque wrench on a busbar lug bolt and torque it to the click
instruction: Pick up the torque wrench standing on its rest, seat its socket fully on the lug bolt, and torque the bolt with it. The wrench is already set to the bolt's torque. Then let go.
context: Electricians and panel builders torque lug and terminal bolts to the value marked on the device with a calibrated torque tool; the US code (NEC 110.14(D)) requires one where marked. The tool starts in hand, off the bolt, its handle resting on the work as fitters do: the socket must be seated square and fully over the hex before pulling, or the socket cams off and rounds the head while the joint stays loose. Click-wrench instructions say: pull steadily at the grip and stop the moment the wrench clicks. The wrench does not limit torque, it only signals it: pulling on through keeps tightening, past the joint's +10 % tolerance, and an over-torqued screw stretches or the lug cracks. Tightening motion before full seating, or pulling through the click, scores 0. Abilities tested: seat a socket on an 8 mm hex before loading it, then stop a steady pull on a one-shot signal from the tool. Done by: electricians (~780k US) and electrical equipment assemblers (O*NET 47-2111.00, 51-2022.00).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left). The joint: a copper flat bar 20 x 6 mm, 12 cm long, on two glass-polyester standoff insulators 2.4 cm tall, runs from x 21 to 33 at y 0. On it, a tinned-copper tube lug for 16 mm2 (about 6 AWG) cable with an M5 hole (palm 18 x 12 x 3 mm, barrel 8 mm across), its cable (black PVC, 8 mm over the insulation) leading off forward. The bolt: M5 x 0.8 x 16 mm hex, class 8.8 zinc-plated steel, ISO 4017 head (7.88 mm across flats, 3.5 mm high, chamfered crown), with an ISO 7089 flat washer, vertical at x 24, y 0, through the lug and bar into an M5 self-clinching nut in the bar; it is a free body on its thread, driven only through the hex. The lug and the panel label are marked 3 N*m (the label is not modelled). The bolt starts snug, at 1.5 N*m (README). The tool: an adjustable click-type torque wrench (chrome-vanadium steel, 1/4-inch square drive, 2-10 N*m range, ISO 6789 Type II class A, +/-6 %), 26 cm long, set to 3 N*m. Under its drive is a low-cost 1/4-inch digital peak-torque adapter (Eclatorq TD2-030CN or equivalent: 1.5-30 N*m, 0.01 N*m resolution, +/-3 % clockwise, peak-hold mode), then an 8 mm 6-point socket (ISO 2725-1; opening 8.2 mm across flats, 0.16 mm clearance per flat, 0.8 mm 45-degree mouth chamfer, 12 mm OD, 25 mm long). A high-contrast radial marker on the wrench head and a fixed reference marker on the busbar are visible to a top camera; a synchronized side camera views the socket rim and washer. Both record at 20 Hz or faster so engagement and wrench-head yaw can be checked in the same frames. Steel fit surfaces have friction 0.3; only the rubber grip is grippy. A second block (9.8 x 4 x 9.7 cm tall) stands under the handle's pull arc beside the joint, its top level with the seated grip's underside: it carries the grip whenever the wrench is on the bolt. The wrench STARTS OFF THE BOLT, standing socket-down on the bench at x 30, y 6, its handle toward the right arm (-y), the rubber grip resting on a 6.3 cm block; the simulated head, adapter, interfaces and socket total a conservative 450 g, with a 100 g handle on a pivot in the head 4.5 cm from the socket axis, held in line by a sprung detent; the grip's load mark 21.5 cm from the axis, so 3 N*m takes 14 N there. Seated on the bolt the wrench's centre plane is 10.6 cm above the table. The simulation uses the full real force and torque: 100 % of the set torque at 4.9 deg past snug, 110 % at 5.9 deg, yield at 230 % (17.7 deg), and the wrench clicks under approximately 14 N at the grip.
scoring: Seated: at least 2.8 mm of the head's 3.5 mm inside the socket, socket axis within 8 deg of the bolt's and 1 mm of coaxial, held 5 control steps; measured from the two bodies' poses. Pre-seat tightening gate: when at least 1.0 mm of the head is inside the socket with tilt at most 12 deg and coaxial error at most 3 mm, record the wrench-head marker angle. Until Seated latches, 1.0 deg or more of wrench-head rotation from that angle is a latched fail. In the sim this is the wrench-head pose; in a real trial synchronized side/top video shows engagement and marker yaw. This measures the wrench, not bolt motion through an unseated socket. Peak torque P, in % of set torque: on a real rig, the digital adapter's peak-hold reading (100 % = 3 N*m); in the sim, the bolt's tightest turn past snug (100 % at 4.9 deg, 110 % at 5.9 deg). After seating, top-camera wrench-head yaw independently measures bolt turn because the hex is keyed. Clicked: the detent broke over (handle bent 1.5 deg) while seated, visible in video. Fail, latched for the trial (score 0): pre-seat tightening; P over 110 %; or a joint that reached the torque band was then backed off more than 3 deg from its tightest. Score: 1.0 for seated click, P 90-110 % (2.7-3.3 N*m), bolt within 1 deg of its tightest; else 0.25 if at least 1.5 deg past snug; else 0.1 for seated but never turned; else 0. Halved unless both grippers are at least 10 cm outside the wrench bounding box and bolt and grip are still (under 0.05 deg and 0.3 mm per step). 1.0 is success, held 1 s. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Back the bolt off (fit a new bolt if its peak went over 110 % or the head was rounded); run it down by hand, then to 1.5 N*m shown by the same digital adapter, align the camera markers at the snug zero, clear the adapter's peak memory, check the click wrench at 3 N*m against that adapter, and stand the wrench back on its bench rest, socket down, grip on the block, handle toward the right arm.
fidelity: Hex/socket use convex contacts with 0.16 mm/flat clearance, steel friction 0.3 and grip 1.2; torque reaches the bolt only through contact. The friction-hinge bolt models 3 N m set torque, 14 N grip load and the rising torque-angle curve. A sprung break-over hinge clicks within 90-110% torque. The 1 deg pre-seat gate measures visible wrench-head motion after 1 mm engagement in both sim and synchronized real video; it does not infer unseated bolt motion. Ratchet internals are not modelled.
